Cormac, whose bakery faced his across the square, happened to be waiting for liniment. The week before, Cormac had learned that Darius refused to undercut his bread prices during the flour shortage. Now I saw Cormac read the label aloud, then pause and read it again more slowly, correcting “three spoonfuls” to “three small spoonfuls,” as the chemist had written in his cramped hand. Afterward the two men walked out together into the sleet, arguing about rye.

When the boats come in at dawn to the harbor in Hanoi,

and the landlord's scale is always kind to the landlord.

On my first morning, Thida showed me the lemon tree by the well, a graft she had bound to a wild root years earlier. The scar still showed, a pale ring where the two barks had met and refused, for a season, to agree. I said I did not know how long I would stay. Thida only tightened the old twine around a new cutting and told me grafts take best when no one watches them too closely. Each evening after that, Zaynab, I told myself, go and see the tree, and I walked to it before supper, pressing my thumb against the ring as if checking a pulse. items.passage: Ramses Station, in the autumn of 1987, kept a narrow cafe beside platform four where students waited out the delays over sweet tea. Yasmin went there every Thursday to pay Karim, her younger brother's tutor, from an envelope she counted twice. He always refused the last coin, pressing it back into her palm with a joke about inflation. She never argued; instead she slipped it into a chipped glass jar on the counter, where the waiter collected change for the boy who swept the platforms. Neither of them ever spoke of it. By spring the jar was nearly full, its coins dull from handling, and the boy was wearing a pair of new shoes. When the trains at last ran on schedule again, the cafe rearranged its tables, but someone kept the jar beside the register.

items.passage: When Camila found the photograph in the drawer of my sea chest, she carried it out to the orchard where I was sitting among the dead mango trees. In the picture I was twenty, grinning on the deck of a freighter, an arm around a man I had not spoken of in forty years. She asked who he was. I told her the trees had stopped bearing the summer I came home, as if they had waited for me and then given up. She did not let me change the subject. She set the photograph on my knee and waited. For a while the memory sat in my chest like an anchor dropped in deep water, heavy and impossible to haul up alone. Then, slowly, with her still beside me, I began to tell her about the storm off Veracruz. Camila listened, peeling a dry branch into strips, while the wind moved through the bare limbs overhead.

items.passage: What does a town do when its two oldest customs both claim the same evening? In the Riga suburb where I grew up, the answer was worked out in 1991 at the back of Vesna's shoe repair stall, because she was mayor and the stall had the only table long enough. Pavel, the town's only doctor, wanted the midsummer supper to follow his family's Orthodox fast; Vesna's neighbors wanted the old Latvian songs and the cheese with caraway. For an hour they argued over awls and heel nails. Then Pavel took a needle from the bench and said the problem was simple stitching. Two leathers of different grain, he explained, can still be sewn into a single sole if the thread is patient. By midnight they had a menu that served both. I still keep a pair of shoes resoled at that stall, and the seam has never split.

At every wedding we staffed in Thessaloniki that summer of 1872, he walked the hall twice before the guests arrived, tapping each chair back and muttering numbers, and I, newly hired, trailed behind him trying not to smile. That evening the hall was so crowded that the count fell apart at once; guests perched on window ledges, and the musicians spilled onto the stairs. I expected an outburst. Instead Hasan stood still among the dancers, and something in his face loosened. He told me, quite softly, that his father had been a foreman too and had once been dismissed because a single guest went without a seat. Then he handed me his tally slate. Keep it or break it, Sadia, he said. Beyond the doors, a cart rolled past on the wet stones.
